## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Alagaddūpama Sutta* ("The Simile of the Snake", MN 22) is the twenty-second discourse of the Majjhimanikāya, set at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove [SuttaCentral; Nance]. The discourse begins when a monk named Ariṭṭha conceives the pernicious view that the obstructive practices warned against by the Buddha—specifically sensual pleasures—are not actually obstacles [Williams et al. 2000; Norman]. Fellow monks and the Buddha subject Ariṭṭha to a firm rebuke, an interchange distinguished by extensive formulaic repetition in which the erroneous claim is reiterated throughout the narrative frame [SuttaCentral; Norman; Bodhi 2005].
To illustrate the proper and improper approaches to his doctrine, the Buddha presents two famous allegories: the water snake and the raft [SuttaCentral; Williams et al. 2000]. Grasping the teachings superficially for the sake of criticism or debate is likened to catching a venomous snake by its tail, which leads to injury or death; learned properly, the teaching brings welfare [SuttaCentral; Pye]. The Buddha further compares the Dhamma to a raft constructed to cross a river: once the far shore is reached, the raft is meant to be abandoned rather than carried on one's head, showing that even righteous teachings (*dhammā*) must eventually be relinquished, let alone unwholesome views [Williams et al. 2000; Goodwin 2012]. The discourse proceeds to a detailed critique of views of self (*attā*), showing through the formula "this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self" that none of the five aggregates can be taken as self, and refutes the Upanisadic notion that the world and the self are identical and eternal [Williams et al. 2000; Tuske 2017; Ngoc Cuong Le 2018]. The Buddha emphasizes that a Tathāgata liberated from the aggregates cannot be found or traced in the phenomenal world, and concludes by distinguishing different grades of disciples, stating that those who practice according to the Dhamma achieve awakening, while those possessing faith and affection for the Buddha are bound for heaven [Bodhi 2005; Norman; Ngoc Cuong Le 2018].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include discourse versions in the Chinese Madhyama Āgama (MĀ 200) and Ekottarika Āgama (EĀ 43.5, EĀ 50.8), as well as Śamathadeva's Tibetan *Upāyikā* (Up 8.029) and monastic codes such as the Pali Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (Pācittiya 68), Kammakkhandhaka (Kd 11), and Chinese Vinaya texts (mi-bu-vb-pc38, T 1442.39) [SuttaCentral]. The narrative of Ariṭṭha's view also survives in Sanskrit in the *Paṇḍulohitakavastu* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya [Nance]. DharmaNexus corroborates these alignments, identifying substantial cross-language text reuse with the Madhyama Āgama (T 26), the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (D 4094), and the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu*, as well as dense Pali-internal reuse across the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), Kd 11, and the closely related *Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta* (MN 38) [DharmaNexus].
